When to Light Halacha says that the menorah must burn for at least half an hour into the night. Many Yidden have the custom to light after ma’ariv, when it is already nighttime, so they just need enough oil or wax to burn for half an hour. But minhag Chabad is to light the menorah before ma’ariv. So, we make sure that the lights last for at least 50 minutes—20 minutes before nighttime and 30 minutes afterwards. On Erev Shabbos, everyone lights the menorah even earlier—after mincha, before Shabbos candles. So, we make sure that the menorah can stay lit for about 90 minutes: until nightfall begins, and for the full half hour afterwards.

The Menorah Itself If you’ve seen menorahs on coins or on shul walls, you’ve probably noticed that the branches are curved. But have you ever seen the menorah in 770? It has straight branches. That’s on purpose. You see, many people think that the menorah in the Beis Hamikdash had curved branches, but the Rambam and others teach us that they were straight (though only seven, of course). For this reason, Chabad Chassidim are careful that the branches on our menorahs are also straight and not curved.

While many Yidden light their menorahs in a window, minhag Chabad is to light it in a doorway in the center of the house—on the left side, opposite the mezuzah, so we are surrounded by mitzvos! This is how the Rebbeim did it, so this is how we chassidim do it, too.

Once the menorah is lit, we sit nearby and don’t do any work for at least half an hour (especially women and girls). The minhag of the Rebbeim was to learn Torah near the licht. This is because the Yevanim tried to stop us from learning Hashem’s Torah, so when we sit and learn davka near the menorah, we show that we’ve won!

Halalu Some Yidden say Haneiros Halalu as soon as the first light is lit, but our minhag is to wait until we’ve lit all of the lights for that night. Our tune comes from chassidim of the Rebbe Maharash. The Rebbeim would face the menorah while saying these words, and we should, too.

One night of Chanukah many years ago, Ephraim Piekarski was playing dreidel with his friend in the hallway of 770. Suddenly, the door swung open. It was the Rebbe.

He walked over to them and said, “I also want to play.”

Ephraim and his friend stared at the Rebbe in shock and didn’t answer. The Rebbe took a dime from his pocket, put it in the game pile, and told one of the boys to spin for him.

The dreidel landed on a “hey”. The Rebbe smiled, “Really, I could take half the pile, but I will leave it for you.” Then, the Rebbe continued walking out.

Rebbe was so busy, but he still took time to to play dreidel on Chanukah!

The Rebbe instructed parents to give their children gelt each night of Chanukah. On one night, they should give extra. Do you know which one? That’s right, the fifth night! What should we do with our gelt? Baruch Hashem, our parents give us food and clothes, so we don’t need to buy those. Instead, we can use the money for mitzvos! First, give some to tzedakah as ma’aser. Then, use the rest for other mitzvos, especially limmud Torah. We can even give gelt to other children!

The Rebbe encouraged us to give menorahs to Yidden who don’t yet have. We want to make sure everyone can do this mitzvah! The Rebbe even sent chassidim with menorahs to every army base. (As you know from last week’s Mivtzoim Mania!) But handing someone a menorah isn’t enough. We must also teach them how to light. It’s especially important that they know the halachos for Erev Shabbos: light before Shabbos licht, and don’t handle the menorah once Shabbos starts.

Minhag Chabad is to use olive oil. Children can use candles that will burn for enough time. (See next section for how long!) Our minhag is to use beeswax candles for the shamash. Beeswax lights easily and burns brightly.

Many Yidden have the custom to put on Shabbos clothes when lighting the menorah, but our minhag is to wear regular clothing. Married men wear a gartel.

Chanukah is an important time for children to get together. This minhag traces back to the Alter Rebbe, who would gather the family and tell special stories on one night of Chanukah. This was called a “-לאַטקֶעס אָוֶוענט—latkes evening,” and was also done by each of the Rebbeim. The Rebbe encouraged us to do the same. Let’s get together on Chanukah to share stories, songs, and the simcha of Yom Tov!

How tall is the biggest menorah in the world? A whopping 32 feet high! That’s just under 20 amos (the tallest possible height for a kosher menorah)—as tall as two giraffes! This giant menorah is lit in Manhattan to fulfill an important part of Chanukah: “נִיסָא פִּרְסּומֵי—to let everyone know about the miracle.” We don’t just celebrate at home, but also in public for all to see. The Rebbe encouraged everyone to arrange public menorah lightings. Nowadays, they’re all over: in malls, parks, and even the White House! These lightings have a huge impact. The Rebbe said that he knows hundreds, even thousands, of Yidden whose neshamos were awakened through a public menorah lighting. Be sure to join one this year! Who knows how many Yidden will be affected? Remember: Public lightings don’t fulfill our individual mitzvah. We still must light at home.

Listening to the Licht The Frierdiker Rebbe explains that we should listen to the message of the Chanukah lights. The story of Chanukah is full of holy and important lessons, and the flickering flames are like its storytellers. What messages can you “hear” while watching the precious lichtelach?

Chanukah is here! For eight days, Yidden all over the world light menorahs to celebrate our miraculous victory over the

Yevanim. As Chassidim, we have special minhagim for how

to light the menorah, and hora’os from the Rebbe about spreading the light of Chanukah all around us: from public menorah lightings to mivtzoim, rallies, and more. Let’s learn

You probably know that Chanukah starts on Chof-Hey Kislev. But do you know what else happened on that day? On Chof-Hey Kislev, the Yidden in the midbar finished building the Mishkan! Although it was celebrated on Rosh Chodesh Nissan, we remember this special occasion during Krias HaTorah each day of Chanukah. We read about the gifts that the nesi’im brought during the Chanukas HaMishkan. The Rebbe explains that we can learn lessons from each nasi and when he brought the presents. Sitting near the Chanukah licht is the perfect time to share words of Torah with your family. Here are eight messages you can say, one for each night:

It’s very hard to be the first one to do something; to be brave when no one else is. But that is exactly what Nachshon ben Aminadav, the nasi of Shevet Yehuda, did. He was the first to have mesiras nefesh and jump into the Yam Suf before it split. On the first day of Chanukah, we read about the karban of Nachshon ben Aminadav. This reminds us to be brave and spread Yiddishkeit even in ways that no one else has done it yet.

Three is the number of shalom. Let's explore why: One of something isn’t shalom—it's just one idea. Nothing to make peace with. Two isn't shalom either, because it’s two ideas against each other. Only when we have a third idea can there be balance that includes the other two ideas, showing that they actually agree with each other! That's true shalom. Chanukah is also shalom. It's not just about the Torah’s light (1), and it's definitely not about the Yevanim fighting the Torah with darkness (2). It's about darkness itself being lit up with the Torah's light (3). Both sides are included. We learn this from the nasi of Zevulun, whom we read about on Day Three. Zevulun didn't stay in the beis midrash learning Torah. He went out and lit up the world with the Torah's light. He brought true shalom, and we can learn from him to do the same.

Did you know that Hashem gave each of us a superpower? That’s right! We have the power to change bad into good; to turn an aveira into a mitzvah! We activate this superpower through teshuva. The first person to do complete teshuva on his own was Reuven. After he moved his father, Yaakov’s, bed without permission, Reuven did teshuva for many years. On the fourth day of Chanukah, we read about the nasi of Reuven and are reminded about our superpower. Let’s use this power today to fix any aveiros and come even closer to Hashem!
